posts.title: Someone Always Has It Worse
posts.excerpt: I went to a basketball game at Marquette this past weekend and got up close to the players. Most days, my body feels like a normal body. That's because I'm...
posts.html:
I went to a basketball game at Marquette this past weekend and got up close to the players.

Most days, my body feels like a normal body. That's because I'm usually around people close to my height. Next to the players, it felt small.

Same body. Nothing about it had changed. Only the comparison had.

Here's what I noticed. The measurement was accurate. They really are taller. But the meaning I gave it was optional. My mind jumped from "they're taller" to "I'm small," and that jump felt like a fact. It wasn't.

Leaders do this with their work all the time.

Self-sacrificers use comparison to take things on. "Others have it worse, so I'll handle it." "They're so busy." "They do more than I do." "It's not that big a deal."

Self-focusers use it, too. "I'm better at this." "It's faster if I do it." "They're not ready."

The direction is different. The move is the same. We measure ourselves up or down against someone, and the measurement hands us a reason to carry what isn't ours.

But comparison does more than justify. It protects an identity. The sacrificer's is I'm the strong one, and others have it worse. The focuser's is I'm the capable one, and they're not ready. Comparison keeps that picture intact. And the cost is that you never find out who you are without it.

Keep that going for years, and you become the person who can't say no, or can't let go. You call it who you are. The sacrificer ends up depleted and unnoticed. The focuser ends up alone with a team that stopped reaching in.

A basketball team doesn't ask everyone to be the tallest. It needs the tall ones, the quick ones, and the ones who see the floor. Nobody's strength takes anything from anyone else's.

That's all-in partnership. It's BOTH/AND. Nobody has to be the best, or the most burdened, to belong. The work goes to whoever it's right for.

So here's an invitation. The next time you hear yourself say "others have it worse" or "I'm better at this," pause. Set the comparison aside and ask: whose work is this, and what do I want?

Then ask the harder one: who would I be if I stopped needing someone to have it worse, or be less ready, than me?

posts.title: She Had a Good Reason to Stay Quiet
posts.excerpt: You have something you want to say, and you've decided it's not worth the risk. A client of mine sits on an executive team. Her CEO is confident, successful...
posts.html:
You have something you want to say, and you've decided it's not worth the risk.

A client of mine sits on an executive team. Her CEO is confident, successful, and very easy to follow, as long as you agree with him.

So why would she rock the boat?

It's a fair question. Agreeing works. And she tried the other way once. She advocated for something, and she was dismissed. She took it as proof that she should never ask for anything again.

That makes sense. Most of us would have drawn the same conclusion.

The reasons for staying quiet are usually logical, and most of them are probably valid. There is a real risk in saying the thing. Stick your neck out, and it can get cut off. The tall poppy gets cut down first.

But notice what happened. One no became a rule. A single moment turned into a permanent policy.

One no isn't a verdict. It's information about one moment, one ask, one person on one day.

The belief underneath is that staying quiet is the safe choice. It feels like wisdom. It often started as a flinch.

And it has a price that never shows up on an invoice. It's exhausting, because the wants don't disappear. They go underground, and you carry them every day. It breeds resentment. And it's disempowering, because each time you decide not to ask, you teach yourself you don't get a say.

Keep that up for years, and you can stop knowing what you want. Then no one can build anything with you, including you.

What she didn't have, in the moment she was dismissed, was another option. All-in partnership is always available. It can lead to better solutions, higher buy-in, and ownership spread across more people. But someone has to offer it first.

So here's an invitation. Pick one thing you've decided not to say. Offer it as a partnership, not a demand: "I'd love your thinking on something." And try it first with someone safer than the person who dismissed you. Practice where the risk is low, so your voice has somewhere to come back.

Then ask yourself: who am I becoming if I keep this up?

posts.title: "I Shouldn't Have to Ask"
posts.excerpt: "If I have to ask, it doesn't count." "If they really cared, they'd know." If you're a self-sacrificer, you've probably thought one of these. I hear some...
posts.html:
"If I have to ask, it doesn't count."

"If they really cared, they'd know."

If you're a self-sacrificer, you've probably thought one of these. I hear some version of it from almost every leader I work with.

You notice everyone else's needs without being told, so you assume love means someone does the same for you. But most people can't see a want you've never said. They fail a test they didn't know they were taking, and you end up feeling unseen while carrying everything.

Here's what the rule really does. It keeps you safe. If you never ask, you never risk a no, and you get to stay the one who needs nothing.

A colleague of mine is hosting the holidays and invited a new family. The mom didn't ask, "What can I bring?" She asked, "Can I help you plan the meal?" In other words, "What can I take off your plate?"

My colleague was surprised. She hadn't known that was an option. Her autopilot is to do everything herself. She just invites, guests offer to bring something, and she ends up deciding and assigning.

The mom offered partnership. My colleague had never thought to offer it, or ask for it, herself.

Partnership takes two people saying yes. When you wait to be noticed instead of asking, nobody gets the chance. They get someone easy and pleasant with no needs, and no one can commit to that. You can spend years giving to people who never get to give back, and end up tired, resentful, and alone.

Alone, it doesn't matter. But relationship, partnership, and leadership can't be done alone.

So ask yourself: who am I if I say what I want out loud?

This week, try one small ask, in a way someone can say yes to. "Would you help me plan this?" If that feels like too much, start with, "I'd love your help with something. Do you have ten minutes?"

Then notice what the other person does with it. Someone gets to say yes, and you get to feel chosen instead of unseen.

posts.title: Two Reasons to Send an Email
posts.excerpt: You have a good idea, and you want the people who matter to act on it. A client of mine did too. She was about to send her leadership team an email she'd spent...
posts.html:
You have a good idea, and you want the people who matter to act on it.

A client of mine did too. She was about to send her leadership team an email she'd spent hours on. It was well thought out and logical, with common sense solutions all in one complete message.

She asked me, "Should I send it?"

So I asked her what her intention was. There's an old rule that there are only two reasons to send a memo. One is to confirm something you've already discussed. The other is to upset someone (read: piss someone off).

Which one was this?

She laughed, because she knew. She hadn't discussed it with anyone. And she didn't want to, because sending the email was easier.

Here's the question I'd ask you, too: when was the last time you chose the inbox because the conversation felt risky?

I don't think it's really about efficiency. "Efficient" is often the word we use for avoiding a conversation we're nervous to have. A conversation means someone might push back, and you can't polish it first. An email lets you stay right without being tested.

But she wasn't trying to share ideas. She was trying to influence her leadership team, and influence runs on trust. Nothing erodes trust faster than being surprised.

Picture the leader who opens that email. They read it alone, with no tone of voice and no one to ask. Her ideas may be brilliant, but what they'll remember is how it felt to be handed a verdict.

The email isn't the enemy. It just belongs at the end of the sequence, not the beginning.

  1. Ask for 15 minutes before you write anything.
  2. Share the one idea you're most excited about and ask what they think.
  3. Then send the email, as confirmation of a conversation you've already had.

Now the email has a different job. Nobody is surprised, and she walks into the next meeting with allies instead of reactions.

posts.title: The Dirty Yes
posts.excerpt: The fastest lie I tell is two words long: “Will do.” Someone asks me for a favor. My stomach drops. My mouth says yes anyway. I call that a dirty yes. It...
posts.html:
The fastest lie I tell is two words long: “Will do.”

Someone asks me for a favor. My stomach drops. My mouth says yes anyway.

I call that a dirty yes. It sounds clean. It isn’t.

If you’ve ever said “no problem” while everything in you said the opposite, you know exactly what I mean.

Here’s what I can see: a dirty yes isn’t an accident. It’s doing a job.

Part of the job is being seen a certain way. Generous. Easy. Not difficult. A no feels like it would say I’m selfish or not team player.

The other part is harder to admit. I want to be owed. I want someone to notice what I carry. That’s why I show up resentful. I wasn’t giving. I was investing, and the return never came.

Every dirty yes also teaches people to expect someone who doesn’t exist. Someone with endless room and no limits (boundaries anyone?). And the longer I play her, the harder she is to stop being.

So the dirty yes doesn’t protect the relationship. It borrows against it, and trust is what I’m spending.

Maybe yours sounds like “let me see what I can do.” Maybe it’s a nod in a meeting you already know you’ll regret.

Think about the last yes you gave that your body didn’t agree with. What were you hoping it would get you?

posts.title: You're Not Careful. You're Vague.
posts.excerpt: Someone stretches a rubber band, aims it at you, and holds it there. You don't relax. You flinch. Shut your eyes. Put your hands up. Not for the sting. For not...
posts.html:
Someone stretches a rubber band, aims it at you, and holds it there.

You don't relax. You flinch. Shut your eyes. Put your hands up. Not for the sting. For not knowing when it's coming.

A client of mine works for a leader like that. She doesn't say things directly. She hints. She hedges. She leaves things unsaid that would take the same ten seconds to say plainly.

She thinks she's being careful. Nobody on her team would call it that.

Here's the part worth sitting with if you lead people: you probably don't think of yourself as underconfident either. You think of yourself as thoughtful. Measured. Not wanting to overstate something before you're sure.

Your team doesn't experience your caution as caution. They experience it as never knowing what's coming. So they stay braced. Watching for the tone shift, the follow-up question, the thing you almost said and didn't. That's not a team doing its best work. That's a team managing you.

We talk a lot about overconfident leaders, the ones who bulldoze. At least you know where you stand with them.

An underconfident leader never lets you know where you stand. That's the actual damage. Not what she says. What she never quite finishes saying.

Think of the last thing you hedged on with your team. What would happen if you just said it plainly, today?

posts.title: Every Suggestion Is Also a Verdict
posts.excerpt: I made a suggestion to a friend going through her divorce. Just a side comment, barely a thought. "I don't want to do that," she said. Fast. Flat. Her walls...
posts.html:
I made a suggestion to a friend going through her divorce. Just a side comment, barely a thought.

"I don't want to do that," she said. Fast. Flat.

Her walls went up before I'd even finished the sentence.

Got it, I thought. I overstepped.

It felt like help when I said it. It landed as criticism when she heard it. Same sentence, two completely different things, depending on which side of it you're standing on.

Here's what I didn't want to admit: a suggestion is never just information. It also says something else, whether I mean it to or not. It says, you're not quite doing this right. Even when I don't believe that. Even when I love the person. The suggestion carries the message anyway.

This wasn't the first time I've done this. It won't be the last, if I'm honest. And every time it happens, something small gets spent. A little less of the safety that made her tell me anything in the first place.

If you're in the middle of something hard and someone hands you an improvement, you don't just hear the improvement. You hear that you're currently getting it wrong. That's true even when the suggestion is small. Especially when it's small, because a throwaway comment means it seemed obvious to them, which means my situation looked simple from the outside. It isn't.

I wasn't trying to criticize her. But I wasn't asked, either. And an unasked-for suggestion doesn't get to choose how it's received.

Next time a suggestion is sitting on the tip of your tongue, try this instead: ask "do you want my thoughts, or do you just need me to listen?" Let them answer before you say the rest.

posts.title: The Leader Who Kept Being Right and Kept Losing
posts.excerpt: He spent six hours writing an SOP nobody was going to read. He just didn't know that yet. Something had gone wrong on his team, so he did what he always does...
posts.html:
He spent six hours writing an SOP nobody was going to read. He just didn't know that yet.

Something had gone wrong on his team, so he did what he always does. Sat down, thought it through, wrote it up clean, formatted it, printed it, posted it.

Then he told the team about it.

They didn't follow it.

So he found backup. Articles, videos, proof his SOP was right. He sent it around. Surely once they saw the evidence, they'd get on board.

Still nothing. Weeks of work, repeatedly ignored, and he genuinely couldn't see why. The plan was good. That's not in question. Something else was broken.

If this sounds familiar, here's the uncomfortable part: you might be doing exactly what he was. Building it alone, then spending just as much effort convincing people it's right, and mistaking that second effort for leadership.

Researchers once studied six years of Hollywood pitch meetings to find out what actually gets greenlit. Not the most polished pitches. The ones that left room for the room to shape the idea. People don't back what they're told is good. They back what they helped build.

The SOP was never the problem. The convincing was.

Think about the last thing you built alone and then tried to sell. What would change if you brought the problem instead of the plan?

posts.excerpt: A client of mine runs a team that's stretched thin. Open positions everywhere, nobody to fill them, the people he does have running on fumes. Last session, he...
posts.html:
A client of mine runs a team that's stretched thin. Open positions everywhere, nobody to fill them, the people he does have running on fumes.

Last session, he told me he'd figured it out. He'd built a real plan. Smart, well thought out, the kind of thing that actually could work.

His next move: walk in and tell his team the plan.

I heard the tires skid before he even finished the sentence.

"Whoa, friend," I said.

Knowing me well enough by now, he rolled his eyes. "Put the problem in front of the team and have them think through solutions together," he said.

Because people don't like being told. Even if the idea is great, it feels obligatory instead of empowering.

He already knew. He just hadn't done it.

Here's the part that stings a little if you're the leader: you are not the smartest person in the room. Your team is. All of them, combined, know more about the actual problem than you do alone, sitting in your office building a plan by yourself.

The plan wasn't the problem. His plan was probably good. But a good plan handed down doesn't get the same thing from people that a plan they built gets. One is compliance. The other is ownership.

He didn't need a better idea. He needed to put the problem down in front of his team and let them find one.

Next time you've got the answer, try holding it for one meeting. Put the problem in front of the people it affects. Ask how they'd solve it. See what comes back.

posts.title: She Went From 80-Hour Weeks to 50, Without Losing a Dollar

posts.html:
A friend of mine took over a business four years ago. Over the first few years, she learned something that stopped me when she said it.

"I've learned I'm not that important."

I pushed back. She runs the place. The buck stops with her.

That's exactly the belief she had to unlearn.

As the leader, she assumed every decision was hers to own, which meant every decision had to be defensible. Made the "right" way. The "proper" way. The way that would hold up if someone questioned it later.

So that's how she led. Not from what her team needed, from how it would look.

Eighty-hour weeks, every decision filtered the same way.

Then she started asking instead of deciding. Her team didn't all want the same thing.

One person needed to hear, out loud and often, that she was doing a good job. Another needed to know a mistake wouldn't cost him his job. A third needed flexibility in her schedule more than anything else.

None of that showed up in the "right" way to lead. It only showed up once she stopped performing leadership and started paying attention to the actual humans in front of her.

She adjusted her approach person by person. Not lowering standards. Just meeting each one where they actually were.

Four years later: 50-hour weeks. Same revenue.

Here's the uncomfortable part. If you're leading anyone right now, there's a decent chance you're optimizing for the same thing she was: how it looks, how it holds up, whether it's defensible. Not because you're vain. Because when you believe the buck stops with you, "correct" starts to feel safer than "actually useful to this specific person."

So ask yourself the question she had to face:

Are you leading in a way that would hold up under judgment, or in a way that actually works for the people in front of you?

Those aren't always the same answer. Most of us default to the first one without noticing we're doing it.

posts.html:
It's evening. I'm on the couch. I'm watching strangers on a yacht scream at each other about things that have nothing to do with me.

I've never met these people. I never will. And yet here I am, three episodes deep, fully invested in whether someone gets fired this episode.

I used to think this was just how I unwind. Then I noticed something.

The nights I reach for it hardest aren't the relaxed nights. They're the nights I have something sitting in me I don't want to look at. A want I haven't said out loud. A disappointment I haven't let myself feel yet. A grief I keep meaning to get to.

Watching someone else's drama is easier than sitting with my own life.

It's not just reality TV. It's other people's lives in general.

If you lead a team, you already know this move. You can tell me exactly what's going on for everyone in your last meeting, who's overwhelmed, who's underperforming, who needs a win. Can you tell me what you want for yourself this year?

If you're a spouse, you're tracking your partner's mood before they walk in the door. You know their stress load, their bad days, what they need from you tonight. When's the last time you told them what you needed?

If you're a parent, you know every practice schedule, every teacher's name, every friend group shift. What did you want to be doing with your one life before you knew any of their names?

If you're a neighbor, you've got opinions on the family two doors down. Their renovation, their custody schedule, their new car. What's happening in your own house that you haven't looked at yet?

Different rooms. Same move.

Here's the part that's easy to miss: it doesn't look like avoidance. It looks like virtue.

I don't know if that's true for you. It's been true for me more times than I want to admit.

The overfunctioning leader looks selfless. The tuned-in spouse looks attentive. The involved parent looks devoted. None of that is wrong, and I'm not telling you to stop noticing other people.

I'm asking a smaller question. When all your attention goes outward, what does that leave you not looking at?

posts.title: I Stopped Waiting to Be Asked
posts.excerpt: Four years into a leadership team, and I still hadn’t figured out the one thing everyone actually wanted from me. The role came with real responsibility...
posts.html:
Four years into a leadership team, and I still hadn’t figured out the one thing everyone actually wanted from me.

The role came with real responsibility, leading parts of the program, and an open invitation for feedback on how I led.

I thought I was good at it. Fair. Compassionate. Collaborative.

That was the problem.

I learned I was leaving people confused, frustrated, and uninspired.

I thought building consensus before making a decision was the responsible thing to do. I thought asking permission before taking over an exercise was polite. I thought keeping track of who’d had their turn leading was fair.

Turns out, people didn’t want any of that.

They wanted me to make the decision. Stop asking. Trust my own instincts, and if I believed what I had to offer was valuable, add it, without checking first whether it was okay.

They wanted me to be confident.

I thought being a good leader meant being likeable, agreeable. The consensus-building, the asking, the careful fairness, none of it read as respect the way I meant it to. It read as someone who didn’t trust themselves enough to lead.

Where are you doing this? Where do you soften a decision into a question because it feels more collaborative, when what the room actually needs is for you to just decide?

I’m working with a team right now, and there’s one person I keep coming back to.

Every conversation, they say the right things. “I want more partnership.” “I want us to work as a team.” “I want better flow.”

Then a meeting starts.

They interrupt before anyone finishes a thought. They shoot down ideas before considering them. They lecture the room on how things “should” go. When someone pushes back, they don’t seem to notice how it lands.

What strikes me isn’t the contradiction. It’s that they don’t see it. They’d tell you, honestly, that they want partnership, and they’d mean it. The gap between what they say and what they do isn’t something they’re hiding. It’s something they genuinely can’t see from where they’re standing.

That’s the part I sit with, because if it’s that easy for someone to miss the gap between their intention and their impact, none of us are exempt from it.

So here’s the invitation, not just for them, for all of us: where might the same thing be true for you?

Where do you say you want feedback, but the room goes quiet a little too fast when someone offers it? Where do you say you value someone else’s ideas, but notice how quickly you’re already explaining why yours is better? Not because you’re pretending. Just because, like this person, it’s hard to see the gap from inside it.

I don’t think the fix is trying harder to catch yourself in the moment. That rarely works when you’re the one inside the pattern. It’s more likely to come from someone who can see what you can’t: a partner, a coach, a teammate willing to name it when your words and your behavior split.

That’s usually the only way any of us close a gap we didn’t know we had.

posts.title: Communication Isn’t the Problem. It’s the Alibi.
posts.excerpt: “Communication” is rarely the problem. It’s usually the alibi. You’ve sat in that meeting. "We just need to communicate better." So you add a status update...
posts.html:
“Communication” is rarely the problem. It’s usually the alibi.

You’ve sat in that meeting. "We just need to communicate better." So you add a status update. Another sync. A shared doc nobody opens. Weeks later, the tension’s still there. Someone’s still defensive. Something you already said twice still didn’t happen.

Here’s why. Being specific is exposing

“I need you to own this project more” is safe. It’s one-sided, so nothing can really be negotiated, argued with, or failed, at least not obviously.

A real agreement is two people putting their actual wants on the table. Say what you want: "I want to know what’s happening on this project so I’m not surprised." Let them say what they want: "I want to give you that information in a way that’s easy and doesn’t take up my whole day." From there, you land somewhere real: status updates every Friday at noon, with a commitment to flag anything going off course early. That version can be agreed to, because there was something specific enough to say yes to.

“Own it more” skips all of that. Nothing specific was ever put on the table, so nothing was really agreed to. It was just nodded at. That gap between what was nodded at and what each person actually meant is what turns into tension, defensiveness, or resentment.

Just one question that is worth keeping close: is this agreement clear enough that a 10 year old could tell us whether we honored it?

Get specific enough to pass that test, and the agreement takes care of itself. The communication was never the problem.

If “we need to communicate better” keeps coming up on your team, this might be why.

You keep handing your team podcasts, posts, programs. Good ones. The kind that changed how you think.

And you keep waiting for the shift. The initiative. The ownership.

It doesn't come the way you expect.

Here's the belief that was quietly running the show: if I just find them the right resource, they'll get it. Made sense. Felt generous, even. But it was never true. I believed it for years before I saw what it actually was, convincing people, just with better manners. The podcast, the post, the program, those were my wants on the table. Nobody asked what was on theirs.

And here's the thing about humans: we don't resist growth. We resist growth that gets decided for us.

So the belief had to go before the behavior could change. I stopped handing over answers and started handing over choices. Three resources instead of one assignment. "What would actually move you forward?" instead of "here's what will."

Same standard. Same direction. Different hands on the wheel.

The team that shows up now isn't nodding along to my plan. They're defending their own.

If your team isn't stepping up, check the belief before you blame the person. You might be surprised what you find sitting underneath it.

posts.title: Good at Their Jobs. Can’t Stand Working Together.
posts.excerpt: One of them overfunctions. Someone’s out. They cover it. A gap opens. They fill it. Before anyone can ask, they’ve already handled it. The other...
posts.html:
One of them overfunctions.

Someone’s out. They cover it. A gap opens. They fill it. Before anyone can ask, they’ve already handled it.

The other underfunctions, in their own way.

They trust people to do their jobs. Wait for someone to ask for help. Don’t step in until they’re invited.

They’re both good at their jobs. They can’t stand working together.

Notice where each one is looking. One is watching the gaps. The other is watching for permission. Neither one is looking at what they actually want.

I asked the overfunctioner what they wanted.

“I want them to just see what needs doing, without me having to ask.”

I asked the underfunctioner.

“I want to know it’s actually okay to jump in.”

At the end of year long leadership development program, I run an exercise called “closing the loop.”

Everyone in the room shares what should have happened differently. What didn’t work. Where the program let them down.

My job is specific: listen openly, validate what they’re raising, own the part our organization played. No defending. No “well, actually.” Just receive it.

Here’s what doing this year after year has taught me. You cannot absorb a room full of criticism while protecting your competence at the same time. Those two things are mutually exclusive. Pick one.

If I walk in protecting how good I am at this, every piece of feedback becomes an attack. I’ll feel the sting of fault, of not being enough, of disappointing people who handed me a year of their development. And I’ll get defensive in about four seconds, no matter how much I want to seem open.

So I don’t walk in protecting that. I walk in with one question doing all the work: how can we be better? Not “was I good enough.” Not “is this fair.” Just: what’s true, and what do we do with it.

From there, something shifts. The exact same words that would otherwise land as blame stop stinging. I’m not contracted. I’m expansive. Curious instead of cornered.

Here’s where this stops being a story about a workshop.

If your team has started talking about you instead of to you, this is almost certainly why. Somewhere, they brought you something hard, and you weren’t standing in that expansive place. You were defending. Maybe you didn’t even notice. You just explained, justified, found the reasonable exception.

They noticed. They always notice.

Going around you became safer than going through you. That’s not a verdict on their loyalty. It’s a verdict on what they learned from watching you receive the truth, once.

Most advice here stops at “create psychological safety.” That’s a slogan, not a shift. It doesn’t tell you what to actually do in the four seconds after someone says something hard about you, or about a person you trusted.

What to do is this: decide, before the moment comes, which place you’re going to stand. Cornered, protecting your competence. Or expansive, in partnership with whatever’s true.

You don’t have to wait for them to bring it either. Ask directly. Request the version of feedback they’ve been trading with each other instead of you.

This week:

And what’s one thing you could ask your team this week, that invites them to bring you the truth directly, instead of waiting for them to decide you’re ready?

His CEO friends all told him the same thing: just delegate.

He already knew how. Assigning a task, explaining it clearly, handing it off cleanly. None of that was the gap.

He just didn’t do it. And no one could tell him why, including him.

Here’s what we found underneath: delegating didn’t feel like sharing a load to him. It felt like moving a burden off his back and onto someone else’s. His team was lean. Every time he pictured handing work off, it felt like he was crushing someone.

So “just delegate” wasn’t bad advice. It was advice aimed at a symptom, while the actual disease sat untouched underneath it.

The belief running the show: the leader absorbs all the pressure. All of it. 

If that’s true, delegation isn’t sharing. It’s inflicting. And no framework, no matter how good, survives contact with a belief like that. He could’ve been handed the best delegation system on the planet and still found a reason to carry the work himself, because the system never touched the actual obstacle. It just gave him a new way to avoid the real one.

This is the part most advice gets wrong, for high performers especially:

  • “Just delegate” assumes the gap is a skill.
  • “Just set boundaries” assumes the gap is courage.
  • “Just ask for help” assumes the gap is knowledge.

Often the real gap is a belief, and a belief doesn’t respond to a tactic. It responds to being named.

Treat the symptom, and the symptom comes back. Different week, different task, same exhausted founder doing the work of three people and wondering why the advice “isn’t working” again.

The question that actually moves something isn’t how do I delegate better.

It’s: what does handing this off mean to me?

For him: I’m transferring my burden onto them.

Once that was on the table, the work changed. Not a better system. A different relationship to what leading requires. He didn’t need a new skill. He needed to stop believing that carrying everything alone was the price of the job.

For this week:

Where has the standard advice never worked for you, no matter how many times you’ve tried it?

That’s usually not a sign you need to try harder. It’s a sign there’s a belief under the symptom that hasn’t been named yet.

Last issue we talked about the moment you cross your own boundary. You set a rule for yourself: no emails after five. An email arrives. And in about thirty seconds, an inner argument plays out and you open it anyway. Nobody forced you. No one was even watching. You talked yourself into it, with a very good reason.

That is what I want to talk about today. The reason is always good. Responsible, even. That is not a coincidence. That is how this works.

Your brain is not trying to sabotage you. It is trying to protect you from discomfort. The moment you feel the pull to cross a boundary, your mind goes looking for cover. And because you are a conscientious person, the cover it finds is conscientious too.

This one is time sensitive.

They are counting on me.

I will not be able to relax until it is handled.

All of those can be true. All of them can also be your brain handing you permission to avoid sitting with discomfort. The justification is not proof that crossing the boundary is the right call. It is proof that your mind is doing its job.

Here is the practice.

When the justification arrives, before you act, ask yourself one question:

How is this reason giving me permission to cross my own boundary?

Not whether the reason is valid. It probably is. The question is what the reason is doing for you. It is giving you cover. It is making it feel responsible, even necessary, to do the thing that relieves the discomfort. Once you can see that clearly, the reason loses some of its power. It is still there. It is still reasonable. But now you can see it for what it is: permission you are writing for yourself.

You do not have to argue with the reason or prove it wrong. You just have to recognize it for what it is: reasonable, and not actually the point.

You made your decision before the email arrived, before the reason showed up, before any of this started. That version of you was not less informed. She was just less uncomfortable.

Trust her.

Nobody is standing over you. It is just you, alone, losing an argument with yourself in under thirty seconds.

Last time, we talked about what boundaries actually are: quiet decisions you make for yourself, not declarations you make to other people. You do not announce them. You just live by them. Simple enough in theory.

Then 5:03pm arrives. An email lands. And something remarkable happens.

A trial begins.

INTERIOR MONOLOGUE | DURATION: 28 SECONDS

Voice 1: This one is important. I should just take a quick look.

Voice 2: You said no emails after five. That was the whole point.

Voice 1: I know, but this is different. It will only take a second.

Voice 2: You said that last Tuesday.

Voice 1: They will think I am unreliable. I will seem checked out. I will just respond and then I am done.

Voice 2: ...

Voice 1: It is one email.

You open the email. The boundary is gone. And here is the thing: nobody made you do that. No one was standing behind you. No one even knew you had a boundary to break. The whole trial was internal, the verdict was yours, and Voice 1 won again.

It works the same way at the end of the workday. You are wrapping up, genuinely ready to stop, and someone drops by or sends a message: one more thing. The courtroom opens. It is quick, it is urgent, it would be rude not to. And twenty minutes later you are still at your desk, vaguely resentful, wondering how this keeps happening.

The boundary was not the problem. You knew exactly what you needed. The gap is the thirty seconds between the trigger and the choice, and what you do inside it.

Notice that Voice 1 always has a reason. A good one. The reasons are never petty or lazy. They are responsible, considerate, professional. That is what makes them so hard to argue with. The justifications do not run out. If you are waiting for a moment when there is no good reason to cross your boundary, that moment is not coming.

Holding a boundary is not about having a stronger argument. It is about being willing to sit with the discomfort of not acting. To feel the pull, the anxiety, the guilt, the what ifs, and let it be there without doing anything about it. That discomfort is brief. It passes. And on the other side of it is the thing you said you wanted: an evening that is actually yours.

The courtroom will always convene. You just do not have to keep ruling against yourself.

Allison

Then I noticed people slowly distancing themselves from me. And I couldn’t figure out why.

It wasn’t because they didn’t like me.

Working alone feels efficient right up until it doesn't. The cost of operating in a vacuum isn't paid by you. It's paid by everyone around you.

Here's a scenario most of us have lived through: You've been working on something for weeks. You've thought through the angles, weighed the options, made a decision. Then you bring it to your team or your partner or your client and the energy in the room goes flat.

They're not excited. They're not impressed. They're surprised. And not the good kind.

You did everything "right." You worked hard. You were thorough. And somehow the result still landed like a thud.

That's the vacuum problem. And it shows up everywhere in teams, in families, in organizations, in ourselves.

THE COMFORT OF WORKING ALONE

Let's be honest: working alone is easier. You move faster. There are no scheduling conflicts. No one pokes holes in your idea before you've fully formed it. No one misunderstands your thinking or takes it somewhere you didn't intend. You're in full control of the process start to finish.

That efficiency is real. It's also a trap.

Because the moment you close the loop, the moment you show your work, roll out your plan, announce your decision, you're no longer working alone. And everyone who wasn't in the room is now experiencing the output of a process they had no part in.

Working in a vacuum doesn't protect your process. It just delays the collision between your thinking and everyone else's reality. 

SURPRISES ARE A RELATIONSHIP TAX

When we surprise someone, even with something good, we're implicitly telling them: I made this decision without you.

For a team member, that might mean: I didn't think your perspective was worth including. For a client, it might mean: I assumed I knew what you needed. For someone you love, it can mean: I handled this, so you didn't have to be involved.

Some of those feel okay in the moment. Most of them accumulate. Over time, the pattern of being surprised, of repeatedly finding out about things after they're already decided, quietly erodes trust. Not dramatically. Just steadily.

You're probably operating in a vacuum if you regularly hear phrases like:

  •    "I didn't know that was happening."
  •    "Why wasn't I looped in?"
  •    "I wish you'd talked to me first."
  •    "I would have told you that wasn't going to work."

THE UPFRONT INVESTMENT PAYS OFF

Bringing others into the conversation costs something. It takes more time. It requires you to sit with uncertainty longer before you've got a polished answer. You have to be willing to let your half-formed ideas be seen, and to let someone else's thinking change where you end up.

That's the work. And most people avoid it not because they're selfish, but because it's genuinely harder than just deciding and executing.

But here's what that investment actually buys you:

  •  Better options, because you didn’t have all the information alone.
  • Faster implementation, because people who shaped the decision are invested in it.
  • Fewer surprises, because everyone already knows where you’re going.
  • More trust, because people feel like they’re part of something rather than subject to it.

Collaboration isn't about consensus or committees or death by meeting. It's about not treating your own perspective as the whole picture when it never is.

THE WORST THING YOU CAN DO

The worst thing we can do to our team members, our customers, our loved ones is to consistently surprise them. Not because the surprise itself is always harmful, but because the pattern signals something. It says: I don't need your input. I don't factor you in until I'm ready to present. You exist at the end of my process, not inside it.

People can forgive a bad decision. They recover from mistakes. What's harder to recover from is the feeling of being managed instead of included. Of being surprised instead of consulted.

The goal isn't to make perfect decisions. It's to make decisions with people so that whatever comes next, you're facing it together.

WHERE TO START

“I’ll just do it.”

“It’s fine.”

“I’ve got it.”

It shows up in small ways.

Picking up the garbage and feeling annoyed.

Reworking your schedule and thinking, must be nice.

Saying yes, then wondering why no one else did.

Trying to convince instead of asking.

Doing it yourself because it’s faster.

Same move = Operating alone.

Underneath it is a quieter belief. If I’m needed, I belong. So we step in without thinking.

We don’t ask.

We don’t pause.

  • others step back

Ask what others want.

Let people carry their part.

Stay close without taking over.

When we dismiss acknowledgment, people do not know what is landing.

When we chameleon, people do not know who they are working with.

Many leaders think resentment is an anger problem.

It’s not.

In Atlas of the Heart, Brené Brown explains that resentment doesn’t actually live in the anger family of emotions.

It lives in the envy family. Which makes sense when you look closely.

Resentment often sounds like:

• “Must be nice.”

• “I guess I’ll just do it myself.”

• “No one else seems to care as much as I do.”

• “Why am I always the responsible one?”

That’s not pure anger. That’s the quiet feeling that others seem to have permission you don’t.

Permission to say no.

Permission to rest.

Permission to ask for help.

Permission to let something be someone else’s problem.

Many of the high-capacity leaders I work with don’t think they’re resentful. They think they’re responsible. But when we keep overriding our own limits, something inside us notices. And eventually it whispers:

“How come everyone else gets to live differently than I do?”

That whisper is resentment.

Not because we’re bad people. But because we’re violating ourselves.

The good news is resentment is incredibly useful data. It’s a signal that something important inside you wants attention.

A want.

A boundary.

A truth you haven’t spoken yet.

Instead of judging the feeling, try getting curious. Where in your life do you notice the quiet thought:

“Must be nice…”

That’s usually where a conversation with yourself needs to begin.

Resentment quietly suffocates leadership.

It drains energy. It limits collaboration. It keeps us operating alone.

But when leaders learn to notice it early, something shifts. They stop carrying everything themselves and start breathing life back into their leadership.

I was working with a horse who had one very clear preference.

Scratch her collar bones.

If I stopped, she’d nudge me. If I scratched the wrong place, she’d reposition herself.

At one point I said to my trainer, half joking, “She’s kind of high maintenance.”

Without missing a beat she said, “No. She knows what she wants and she’s okay asking for it.”

That hit me harder than I expected. Because in my head, I had already labeled her.

Needy. Demanding. Extra.

And then I realized something uncomfortable.

That’s exactly what I do to myself.

When I want more support.

When I need help.

When I wish someone would step in.

There’s a voice that says:

Don’t be high maintenance.

Don’t be needy.

Don’t make this about you.

So instead of making a request, I make it mean something.

If I ask, it’s a demand.

If they don’t respond, I’m a burden.

If I stop over-functioning, I’m selfish.

But here’s what the horse taught me. A request is just a request. The other person can honor it. Or not.

It doesn’t make you wrong for asking. And it doesn’t make them wrong for declining. It only becomes heavy when we attach meaning.

High performers are very good at skipping the request phase and going straight to resentment. We’d rather go it alone than risk being perceived as high maintenance. And that slowly dilutes our leadership.

Because leaders who cannot ask clearly cannot lead clearly.

Here is a common trap self sacrificers fall into.

They announce a boundary in advance.

"I just want you to know I will not be doing this anymore."
"I am enforcing a new boundary."
"Please respect it."

It sounds healthy, but it's usually avoidance.

The real purpose is not clarity.
It is control.

Boundary warnings are an attempt to prevent future requests so the person never has to say no in real time.

Because saying no is uncomfortable.

So instead of managing themselves in the moment, the self sacrificer tries to manage other people ahead of time.

That is a workaround.

Boundaries are not declarations.
They are choices.

You do not need to warn people about a boundary.
You only need to act when the moment arrives.

"No. That does not work for me."
"I am not available for that."
"I am choosing something else."

If you notice yourself wanting to announce a boundary, that is your signal.

The work is not saying it louder.

Most people get boundaries wrong.

A boundary is not something you explain or enforce on someone else.
A boundary is simply what you will do if you feel a certain way.

That’s it.

No one needs to know your boundary.
No one else is responsible for honoring it.
That part is on you.

Where things go sideways is how we try to protect our boundaries.

When I feel even a little threatened, I notice myself getting rigid and vigilant. I focus on what I won’t do. I brace. I guard. And without realizing it, I change who I am just to hold the line.

Here’s the reframe.

A boundary isn’t only about what you won’t do.
It’s also about what you can do and what you want to do.

When you focus there, boundaries stop feeling like walls you have to defend. They become clearer. Calmer. More human.

Quick example.

Someone asked me for help when I didn’t have the capacity. My instinct was to brace for disappointment or pushback.
Instead, I said, “I can’t help in that way, but I can do this.”

The moment I focused on what I could do, the boundary held without me hardening or pulling away.

Strong boundaries don’t require rigidity.
They require clarity.

posts.html:
High self sacrificers think they struggle to trust other people. And on paper it makes sense. People miss details. They forget things. They drop the ball. So you stay ready to jump in. You build backup plans. You keep everything moving. It feels efficient.

But that is not the real issue.

The real issue is that you do not trust yourself to handle the tough conversations that follow when someone does not follow through.

That is why even small hints of inconsistency create a spike of anxiety. Because if something goes sideways, it is not just inconvenience. It means you might have to say something. Clarify something. Confront something. And that feels harder than doing the work yourself.

So self sacrifice becomes the strategy. Not because others are incapable. But because avoiding tough conversations feels safer than having them.

Here is the good news. Trust is not built by waiting for perfect conditions. Trust is built by practice. Especially the practice of uncomfortable conversations.

When I started working on this, I chose small reps. One tiny tough conversation a day. A simple no. A quick clarification. A small correction instead of swallowing it. Some felt awkward. Here’s the part that surprises most leaders:
Self-sacrifice isn’t a choice. It’s a nervous system loop.

Here’s how it works:

Your brain hates conflict.
Saying “no” feels like danger. Your amygdala (fear center) flares, so you avoid it.

Your body rewards sacrifice.
Every time you say “yes,” your brain gives you a dopamine hit — a quick high for being “helpful.”

Your subconscious locks it in.
Over time, you wire the belief: My value comes from giving more. It runs in the background, automatic, even when you “know better.”

The result? You’re stuck in a cycle. Even when you want to stop, your nervous system pulls you back. You say yes, you neglect your needs, and you call it “just being a good leader.”

But here’s the truth:

  • Self-sacrifice keeps you in survival mode. Your nervous system stays in fight-or-flight.

  • In survival mode, your prefrontal cortex (the rational, strategic part of the brain) goes offline.

  • That’s why smart leaders, people who can solve million-dollar problems, still can’t solve their own exhaustion.

It’s not weakness. It’s wiring.

And the only way out is to rewire: small no’s, nervous system regulation, reclaiming your energy.

Because here’s the kicker: when you break the loop, you don’t lose influence. You gain it. People trust you more when you’re steady, not resentful. They follow your clarity, not your exhaustion.

  • When you stand tall, you give permission for others to stand tall too.

posts.html:
Most leaders think sacrifice means putting others first.

But the most costly sacrifices aren’t obvious. They’re the ones that look like “helping” when really, you’re avoiding.

  • You avoid a tough conversation by fixing someone else’s work.
  • You step over a missed deadline and stay late to clean it up.
  • You ignore your own priorities so you can say yes and keep everyone happy.

It feels generous in the moment. But it’s not.
It’s sacrifice rooted in avoidance.

And here’s the truth: avoidance compounds.
Every time you step over what needs to be said, the weight shifts back on you.
Every time you ignore your own limits, your energy shrinks.
Every time you avoid conflict, you create more of it down the road.

That’s why you’re drained. That’s why resentment creeps in.

When we become a stand for ourselves, everything shifts:

  • We have more energy because we’re aligned instead of divided.
  • We’re more confident because we know how to make and defend our decisions.
  • We serve others more powerfully because authenticity is easier than juggling everyone else’s expectations.

That’s the move from just helping to truly serving.
